rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer addressed Egypt's royal court when Pharaoh proposed killing Moses; after hiding his faith until this decisive moment, he openly revealed it.
rows.anchor: This speech was delivered by the true believer to the House of Lords of Egypt before all the courtiers and nobles.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His royal-family status meant the courtiers could not dismiss his advice as bias in favor of the Israelites.
rows.anchor: he was a noble of the royal family; hence his advice could not have been regarded to be one given in bias for the Israelites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's mention of helping with a third celebrates this nobleman's courageous public support for Moses and the messengers.
rows.anchor: It is this shinning feat and ever-famous exploit of this great person that is mentioned by Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arguments and fearless manner of his defense of Moses have no parallel except among God's prophets and the righteous.
rows.anchor: the fearless nature in which he spoke has no parallel except in the history of prophets of God and the righteous.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural claim to be sent does not make all three equal in rank; it is a collective expression in which the dominant member is implied, like members of one embassy speaking together.
rows.anchor: This linguistic style is one in which the dominant element is implied.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses alone was the primary messenger; Aaron assisted him, while the third man was a courageous supporter who undertook to preach Moses' message and was grouped with the messengers for that work.
rows.anchor: only Moses (sws) was the real messenger. Aaron (sws) too was not the primary messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejecters routinely object that messengers are ordinary humans and that God should choose a superior creature; Pharaoh's court and the Quraysh raised this objection.
rows.anchor: This is the same objection which rejecters of every messenger of God raised.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that the Merciful revealed nothing means the rejecters denied that God had sent the prophet any revelation or Book.
rows.anchor: imply that the Prophet’s claim that God has sent His revelation or Book to him is absolutely false

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers' statement that their Lord bears witness is an oath responding to rejection; the plural messenger wording again reflects the dominant member, as in 36:14.
rows.anchor: In response to the rejection of their respective followers, these messengers swore on oath that they have been sent by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers warn that their duty is only to deliver God's message clearly, not force it on people; rejecters will face the consequences while the messengers have fulfilled their obligation.
rows.anchor: the only responsibility they have from God is to present to them the word of God in a clear and distinct manner; they cannot force it down their throats.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here taṭayyarū means to regard someone or something as a bad omen bringing bad luck.
rows.anchor: Here it means to regard something as a bad omen and one that brings bad luck.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Instead of taking Egypt's calamities as warnings about their own deeds, the people blamed Moses and his followers, claiming their message angered the deities.
rows.anchor: they regarded them be bad omens from Moses (sws) and his followers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They threatened to stone Moses and his companions and cause further harm if they did not stop preaching, ostensibly to protect their deities.
rows.anchor: they will stone them to death in order to protect their deities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He links this accusation to 7:130–131: drought and reduced fruit were sent so Pharaoh's people might heed, but they claimed good times for themselves and blamed Moses and his companions for calamity.
rows.anchor: This topic is also discussed in Sūrah A‘rāf in the following words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭā'ir means misfortune here.
rows.anchor: Here it means “misfortune.” This is the reply given by the messengers: these people try to find the causes of the misfortune in others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers answer that the people's misfortune comes from their own beliefs and deeds, so they should examine themselves instead of blaming others.
rows.anchor: Whatever is happening to them is the result of their own beliefs and deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about being reminded means the people treat the messengers' warning about good and evil as the supposed cause of their bad luck.
rows.anchor: they have been reminded by these messengers and made aware of their good and evil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their arrogance leads them to cross God's bounds and endanger themselves, then blame the very servants who warn them instead of thanking them.
rows.anchor: by crossing the limits set by God they put themselves into danger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man who comes running is the believer from Pharaoh's family discussed in 7:9 and Sūrah Mu'min; these verses show how the third warner of 36:14 helped.
rows.anchor: the true believer who belonged to the Pharaoh’s family

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His home was at the far end of the city, yet his concern for the truth was genuine and practical, unlike drawing-room praise by many elites.
rows.anchor: the sympathy of the true believer was not mere pretension. It was genuine.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When danger threatened Moses, the believer ran to him from far away and risked his interests and life to shield him.
rows.anchor: as soon as he felt danger was lurking for Moses (sws) he ran to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi identifies this as the same episode in which the believer spoke before Pharaoh and his courtiers; the succeeding verses support that identification.
rows.anchor: the one in which he delivered the speech before the Pharaoh referred to earlier. The succeeding verses corroborate my view.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the people to follow the messengers does not mean the believer formally counted himself among them; he urges them to follow God's guides and their supporters instead of Pharaoh, Hāmān, Qārūn, and other evil leaders.
rows.anchor: instead of following the Pharaoh, Hāmān and Qārūn and other evil leaders should follow those whom God has sent to guide people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first reason to follow the messengers is that they seek no reward and endure hardship solely to guide people, unlike self-serving opponents.
rows.anchor: they have no vested interest associated with their preaching; they are enduring all these sorrows purely to guide people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second reason is that they are rightly guided: selflessness indicates sincere intent but does not establish truth, so their message must also be rational; rejecting those meeting both tests is a misfortune.
rows.anchor: being selfless does vouch for a person’s sincere intentions; however, to be sincere in intention does not mean that a person is also rightly guided.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer's defense of worship appears to answer leaders who rebuked him after he urged the people to follow the messengers, treating him as an enemy of their nation and ancestral faith.
rows.anchor: in response to the rebukes of the leaders

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His direct address to the people expresses anger: all will eventually stand before the Lord whose worship they forbid and answer for their deeds.
rows.anchor: is to express anger. The implication is that one day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deities cannot intercede or rescue him if God wills harm, so they are helpless and cannot warrant worship.
rows.anchor: these deities are so helpless that neither can their intercession

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If he worshipped those deities, he would be in manifest error without an excuse.
rows.anchor: an open deviation from the truth for which he has no excuse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His declaration of faith in their Lord decisively answers the people: they should adopt his path and believe in the Lord who is theirs as well, rather than lead him away from God.
rows.anchor: it is better that they too adopt the path which he has adopted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After his public declaration, the people became his enemies and conspired, but God saved him and gave him Paradise; he longed for his people to know why he was forgiven and honored.
rows.anchor: he was given glad tidings of Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The time of the glad tidings is unknown; possibilities include being killed after his declaration or migrating after losing hope in his people.
rows.anchor: Here it is not known when these glad tidings were given to him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed possibility is that God gave him death and the glad tidings after his mission was complete.
rows.anchor: Thirdly, since his mission had been completed God gave him death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Considering the context, he initially finds the possibility that the people killed the believer very probable.
rows.anchor: the first of these options though seems very probable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He then rules out death at the people's hands because 40:44–45 says God protected the believer from their plots; he says the timing remains difficult to decide.
rows.anchor: the option that he was killed is ruled out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The certain point is that God promised him Paradise because he risked his life to support the truth.
rows.anchor: Paradise for endangering his life to support the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'after him' can mean after the believer's death or after his migration, either of the two possibilities under discussion.
rows.anchor: can be spoken for both the options referred to above: ie. after his death or after his migration.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage invokes God's established practice toward a people after a messenger and his companions migrate from them: their rejection is followed by destruction.
rows.anchor: This is a reference to the established practice of God which the rejecters of a messenger necessarily face when the messenger and his companions migrate from their nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God needed no heavenly army to destroy the people; one blast from Him was sufficient to devastate them instantly.
rows.anchor: God did not need to send down any army from the heavens; it was just one blast from God that devastated them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ṣayḥah (cry or shout) signifies punishment.
rows.anchor: The word ةَحْیَص signifies punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording that God was not a sender of armies emphasizes that He needed no such arrangement; a single shout was enough.
rows.anchor: for such a task no such arrangement is need by God; just one blast is enough from Him.
